chunks.citation: Malik, OA et al. (2015). A global indicator of wastewater treatment to inform the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). ENVIRON SCI POLICY.
chunks.text: Wastewater is typically collected through sewage pipes in municipal areas. Treatment of wastewater entails a step-wise process that occurs in primary, secondary, and tertiary stages. Primary treatment involves basic screening and filtration processes to remove suspended solid waste and reduce its biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), which is an indicator to monitor water quality that assesses the amount of oxygen microorganisms must consume to break down the organic material present in wastewater (US EPA, 2012) . Primary treatment can reduce BOD by up to 30% (Flo ¨rke, 2013) . Secondary treatment uses biological processes to break down the dissolved organic matter remaining after primary treatment. Secondary treatment can remove up to 90% of BOD and total suspended solids (US EPA, 2004) . Any additional step in wastewater treatment is considered tertiary treatment (or ''advanced treatment''), which includes any purification process that continues beyond the previous steps and may require more complex technology such as ion exchange and reverse osmosis to further remove contaminants or phosphorous and nitrogen (World Bank, 2013b; US EPA, 2004) .

chunks.citation: Ma, Y et al. (2009). Achieving nitrogen removal via nitrite in a pilot-scale continuous pre-denitrification plant. nan.
chunks.text:
The traditional biological nitrogen removal processes utilized in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) involve the oxidation of ammonium (NH 4 þ ) to nitrate (NO 3 À ) (nitrification) followed by nitrate reduction with an organic carbon source to nitrogen gas (N 2 ) (denitrification). Both nitrification and denitrification possess nitrite (NO 2 À ) as an intermediate. Hence, if

nitrification is stopped at nitrite, denitritation from nitrite to nitrogen gas can be achieved (Verstraete et al., 1977) . Nitrogen removal via nitrite yields 25% reduction in oxygen demand for nitrification and 40% reduction in chemical oxygen demand (COD) requirement for denitrification (Pollice et al., 2002; Turk and Mavinic, 1987) . The reduction in COD requirement would be particularly advantageous for WWTPs treating wastewater with a low COD to nitrogen ratio.

chunks.text: However, these processes are costly, require high energy consumption and generally produce secondary waste which cannot remove the pollutants completely and then puts more pressure on the environment (Ghafari et al., 2008; Kapoor and Viraraghavan, 1997) . In contrast, biological treatment is generally regarded as a better choice for nitrate removal from wastewater due to its advantages of complete contaminants removal, economical and energy-saving. Currently, the complete denitrification process is widely applied for nitrate-containing wastewater treatment (Gu et al., 2015; Song et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020) . However, the traditional complete denitrification process (Eqs. ( 1 ) and ( 2 )) still presents some shortcomings, including high operational costs due to external organic carbon source requirements (Gu et al., 2015; Song et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020) , large amounts of sludge yields and inevitable greenhouse gas emission, etc. (Du et al., 2016b) . Partial denitrification (PD) refers to the process of controlling NO 3 − -N reduced to NO 2 − -N without further reducing to nitrogen gas (N 2 ).

chunks.text: Table 1 shows the inactivation rate constants along with the modelling and observed log reduction values for each of the sampling sites. 95 % confidence intervals were calculated for each location for both observed and modeled disinfection efficacy. Comparing the confidence intervals for the N res value to the Plant LRV from the plant determines if the treatment is system or matrix limited. If the WRRF LRV is significantly lower than the modeled N res then there is a system limitation. If there is no significant difference, then the system is performing at the limitation of the matrix. This comparison of confidence intervals revealed that WWTF-A and WWTF-D s were system limited; whereas WWTF-B and WWTF-C were matrix limited. This aspect of the UV audit provides a robust modelling parameter to compare to effluent LRV when definitively determining system versus matrix limited reactors. This feature of the audit also removes human error in the assessment of plant performance as WWTF-D system limitation was not detected via the initial audit step described in Section 3.1.

chunks.text: The nitritation is a common attempt for generating NO 2 − -N for anammox bacteria. This process consists of two pivots: enrichment of AOB and suppression of nitrite oxidizing bacteria (NOB) by making selective pressure on the two groups of bacteria (Fig. 1 ). The primary strategies for controlling nitritation include low dissolved oxygen (DO) (Laureni et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2013) , high temperature, short sludge retention time (SRT) (Kouba et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2013; Pollice et al., 2002) , real-time aeration control (Gu et al., 2012; Peng et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2007) , as well as the free ammonia (FA) and free nitrous acid (FNA) based sludge treatment (Wang et al., 2016) . However, there are still major issues in the practical application for both of the high-strength wastewater and mainstream treatment.

chunks.text: Nitrogen removal in conventional wastewater treatment is primarily accomplished through nitrification/denitrification (N/DN) (Arumugham et al., 2024) . However, this process requires aeration and carbon sources, and produces CO 2 and N 2 O (Cao and Fan, 2023) . Wastewater treatment facilities produce 1-2 % of society's total carbon dioxide emissions (Zhang et al., 2024b) , and 3 % of global N 2 O (Ramírez-Melgarejo et al., 2020) . In contrast, anammox utilizes nitrite as an electron acceptor to directly convert NH 4 + to N 2 , reducing N 2 O emissions, reducing oxygen consumption by 62.5 %, eliminating the need for carbon inputs, and reducing sludge production by 90 % (Huang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2019a) .

chunks.text: The GAC pilot study was conducted at the municipal wastewater treatment plant Muenchehofe (Berlin, Germany) over a consecutive period of ten months. The WWTP treats up to 42,500 m 3 /d by primary sedimentation, biological activated sludge treatment with chemical precipitation and secondary clarification. Characteristics of the secondary effluent during the experimental period are given in Table 1 . The pilot plant consists of two identical filter columns, each with a diameter of 0.15 m and a height of 4 m. One filter is operated as dual-media downflow filter, whereas the other filter uses only GAC as filter material and is fed in upflow direction. GAC Epibon A 8 Â 30 mesh was supplied by Donau Carbon, Germany. Upon filling the filter columns, the GAC was wetted for two days and backwashed several times to remove undersized particles. The dual-media filter uses 1.4 m GAC and 0.6 m quartz sand (0.7e1.1 mm) as filter material.
